articles.full_text:
EQS Group GmbH/ Key word(s): Miscellaneous
EQS Group receives validation of its climate targets by the Science Based Targets initiative
26.10.2026 / 17:00 CET/CEST
The issuer is solely responsible for the content of this announcement.
Munich – 26 October 2026
EQS Group, a global leader in agentic AI SaaS for compliance, today announced that the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) has successfully validated EQS Group’s near-term and net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction targets.
The Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) helps companies set measurable emissions reduction targets based on climate science. Its Corporate Net-Zero Standard calls for companies to take action in the near term and make deep emissions cuts over the longer term, both in their own operations and across their value chains. SBTi Services, the initiative’s target validation subsidiary, confirmed that EQS Group’s targets for 2030 and 2050 meet these requirements.
Validated targets
- Net-Zero: EQS Group commits to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions across the value chain by 2050.
- Near-Term: EQS Group commits to reduce absolute scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions 85.0% by 2030 from a 2022 base year. EQS Group also commits to reduce scope 3 GHG emissions 51.6% per EUR value added within the same timeframe.
- Long-Term: EQS Group commits to reduce absolute scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions 90.0% by 2050 from a 2022 base year. EQS Group also commits to reduce scope 3 GHG emissions 97.0% per EUR value added within the same timeframe.
Details on EQS Group’s targets are available on the SBTi website.
EQS already sources renewable electricity at its main locations in Germany and Spain, encourages employees to commute by bicycle or public transport, and permits business travel by air or car only in exceptional cases. EQS also reports its greenhouse gas emissions annually.
“Our customers and partners expect the same transparency and accountability from us that we help them achieve,” said Achim Weick, founder and CEO of EQS Group. “Setting science-based targets gives our emissions reduction work a clear direction. External validation provides a reference against which stakeholders can assess our progress. This is part of how we build lasting trust and a resilient business.”
More information about EQS Group’s sustainability strategy, activities and reporting is available on its corporate sustainability page: https://www.eqs.com/about-eqs/sustainability/

EQS Group is a global leader in agentic AI SaaS for compliance. More than 14,000 companies worldwide trust EQS Group to meet complex regulatory requirements, manage risks, and report transparently on business performance and their impact on society and the environment.
EQS Group’s compliance & ethics solutions help organizations build trust, enable secure whistleblowing and manage cases, and address compliance risks. Investor relations teams benefit from solutions that simplify regulatory disclosures and strengthen capital market communication. articles.title: Sustainable finance and biodiversity, Reuss: “The challenge? Connecting data and bringing projects together” - Materia Rinnovabile | Renewable Matter
articles.summary: Sustainable finance and biodiversity, Reuss: “The challenge? Connecting data and bringing projects together”  Materia Rinnovabile | Renewable Matter
articles.full_text:
From risk assessment to the development of financial tools capable of supporting long-term initiatives, biodiversity raises challenges that call for greater integration between finance, public policy and knowledge of ecosystems. We discussed this with Isabel Reuss, Senior Climate and Social Advisor at the Forum for Sustainable Finance, a non-profit organisation founded in 2001 to promote awareness and practice of sustainable and responsible investment in Italy.
As the Forum for Sustainable Finance, in 2024 you published the paper Sustainable Finance and Biodiversity: A Guide for Practitioners. It was at the height of the European regulatory cycle, which subsequently gave way to a phase of simplification. Does this pose a risk to biodiversity finance, or is the market now mature enough to continue even without stringent requirements?
Not everything that is happening should be viewed in a negative light. Regulatory simplification, which must be distinguished from a reversal of regulation, can also have positive aspects, particularly when it helps reduce the costs and burdens associated with data collection and analysis. I also welcome the changes introduced in the SFDR, with the creation of a transition category, as biodiversity must also be understood through this lens: it is useful to recognise that there are not only activities already fully sustainable and those that are not, but also pathways for improvement. The reduction in the information required from companies, for example within the framework of European sustainability reporting standards, is a different matter altogether. If the number of indicators and the number of companies required to report are reduced, important information risks being lost.
Are companies backing away from sustainability reporting now that they are no longer obliged to do so?
Not necessarily. In my experience, companies that already started working on these issues will continue to do so, even if they have to report less data. Other companies are, however, becoming more aware of the risks associated with the natural environment, as the effects of floods, droughts and heatwaves are becoming increasingly evident.
Simplifying, therefore, does not mean taking a step backwards.
No. Simplification does not mean abandoning obligations: awareness amongst operators is growing, but this does not mean that everyone is ready to act independently just yet. Draghi himself spoke of simplification, not deregulation. It is important, however, that simplification does not become a pretext to stop considering risks and impacts. In this regard, another positive aspect I see at this stage (I am referring to the Nature Restoration Law) concerns the opportunity to analyse not only measures that improve the situation, but also those that worsen it. I am thinking, for example, of subsidies and incentives that may have negative effects on biodiversity: if we focus exclusively on how to improve things, without considering what is simultaneously continuing to cause damage, we are unlikely to achieve results.
How have financial operators been operating in recent years?
I see considerable activity in both the insurance and banking sectors, albeit in different ways. The insurance sector is probably where the changes are most visible. Operators are realising that a significant proportion of the damage caused by catastrophic events is not covered by insurance and that, if this situation continues, certain risks could become difficult to insure. Initiatives are therefore being developed at the national and European level to encourage collaboration and data sharing. Tools such as parametric insurance are also being trialled. This is a sign that the sector is seeking solutions to risks it can no longer regard as marginal.
What about the banking sector?
For banks, this shift involves a growing focus on businesses’ dependence on nature and the consequences this may have on financial performance, as shown by a number of major global analyses. This is an important step, as it highlights the link between nature and financial risk. If a business is heavily dependent on a natural resource, the deterioration of that resource can jeopardise its operations and, consequently, its ability to repay a loan. Biodiversity is thus beginning to feature in risk management: it is not merely a question of financing projects that have a positive impact on nature, but also understanding how dependence on ecosystems and the impacts that businesses have on them can influence the risk profile.
Is the volume of investment sufficient to meet requirements?
In this regard, the situation remains concerning. Among the recent figures released by UNEP, one struck me in particular: in 2023, approximately $7.3 trillion was invested in activities harmful to biodiversity, compared with around $220 billion allocated to support biodiversity. Estimates may vary, but the contradiction remains: we continue to allocate vast resources to activities that harm nature, while investments to protect and restore it remain insufficient. This is why I believe the financial gap is still very wide. It is not enough simply to increase positive investments: we must also tackle the financial flows that fuel degradation. This is an aspect that public policies should take into account.
Biodiversity is more difficult to measure than climate, because there is no single indicator comparable to a tonne of CO₂ equivalent. What metrics can financial operators use today?
First of all, a distinction between dependencies and impacts must be made. On one hand, we need to understand the extent to which a business depends on biodiversity and the services provided by ecosystems; on the other, we need to assess the effects its activities have on nature. In any case, I do not believe we will find a single metric applicable to every situation. Those working on biodiversity often tend to look for very specific indicators, suited to describing each individual project. However, when a financial operator has to assess an entire portfolio, they cannot analyse every activity in the same level of detail. We must find ways to aggregate the information and construct summary indicators, or proxies, to enable an initial assessment to be made.
The European project BIO-CAPITAL, in which the Forum for Sustainable Finance is also involved, combines three worlds that do not usually interact: conservation, finance and space technologies. What specific benefits can tools such as geospatial analysis and satellite technologies offer investors?
Satellite data can be very useful, first and foremost, as it enables the collection of large amounts of information about areas and the changes that occur over time. It can help to establish an initial situation, a baseline, against which to assess the effects of an intervention. It can also help to identify certain signs of improvement, but it is important to combine it with other information. In a forest, for example, the first signs of change may relate to the presence of mosses or fungi, even before any significant changes in tree growth become visible. It is important, however, to be aware of the limitations of these tools. A satellite can detect the presence of vegetation, but it is not always able to distinguish a natural forest from a monoculture plantation. From above, both may appear green, but from a biodiversity perspective, they are very different situations. For this reason, satellite data cannot replace all other forms of verification: they must be supplemented with observations and information gathered on the ground.
BIO-CAPITAL also explores the various financing mechanisms for biodiversity, ranging from payments for ecosystem services to biodiversity credits, and from the various forms of blended finance to debt-for-nature swaps. Which of these tools do you consider most promising?
The real challenge is to understand which combinations can lead to economically and financially sustainable solutions. The fundamental problem is that biodiversity can be funded, but often does not generate direct revenue. Such initiatives yield significant benefits, but in many cases these are collective: they do not necessarily translate into a cash flow for investors. It is a crucial difference compared to other investments, as private investors must still assess the balance between return, liquidity and risk. For this reason, I believe that many conservation and restoration projects will need to combine public and private resources, each serving different yet complementary roles.
There is the matter of available resources.
If we want to implement territory-wide projects, as required by restoration strategies, significant funding is needed. But many European countries must contend with the constraints of public debt. We must understand how to allocate funding between the public and private sectors, and which tools can be used to mobilise capital without passing on all the costs to the state budget. Public-private partnerships strike me as an important approach, precisely because they allow us to combine different resources and areas of expertise. However, it is not enough to combine public and private capital: we need to develop models that take into account the risks, the timeframe for implementation and the nature of the benefits generated.
Small scale of projects, lack of cash flow, regulatory uncertainty: what is the main obstacle to the widespread adoption of these instruments?
I think one of the main problems is aggregation. Many projects are small and, taken individually, do not reach the scale required to access the financial market. Large investors, including funds, require tools with a certain level of liquidity. We therefore need to find a way to pool several initiatives together in order to create transactions large enough to be attractive to the market. The question is who can fulfil this role. articles.title: EU Carbon Market Proposal Would Reshape Marine Fuel Economics Unevenly - Global Trade Magazine
articles.summary: EU Carbon Market Proposal Would Reshape Marine Fuel Economics Unevenly  Global Trade Magazine
articles.full_text:
October 26th, 2026 | Written by IndexBox
EU Carbon Market Proposal Would Reshape Marine Fuel Economics Unevenly
Europe’s carbon market may soon begin compensating shipowners for fuel switching, yet the assistance available is anything but uniform. In July, the European Commission put forward a revision of the EU Emissions Trading System that would set aside as many as 110 million allowances from 2028 through 2040 for a new Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion mechanism, designed to bridge part of the cost difference between fossil marine fuels and sustainable substitutes.
Read also: IMO Approves New Safety Guidelines for Ammonia as Marine Fuel
Rystad Energy’s analysis indicates that, taken together with the EU ETS itself and the FuelEU Maritime regulation, the proposal would alter the cost hierarchy of marine fuels across Europe. BioLNG and renewable e-fuels are positioned to benefit most, whereas biodiesel derived from used cooking oil and animal fats, among the most commonly used marine biofuels today, receives no support.
Timing and Compliance Pressure
Timing is significant. Starting in 2026, shipping firms must surrender ETS allowances covering 100% of their verified in-scope emissions, which now include methane and nitrous oxide, while FuelEU Maritime mandates a progressively stricter reduction in the greenhouse-gas intensity of onboard energy use. Both frameworks depend on the sustainability criteria of the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive. For shipowners, charterers and fuel suppliers, the central question is which fuel pathway the combined rules favor.
How the Subsidy Would Work
SMAP would bridge 55% of the remaining price gap to fossil fuel for biogas and advanced biofuels, and 90% for renewable fuels of non-biological origin such as e-ammonia and e-methanol, with an extra 10 percentage points when the feedstock originates in the EU. Since support scales with the size of the gap, the costliest fuels receive the most per tonne, and EU-made e-ammonia could have its entire remaining premium covered. Support is cut in half for voyages entering or leaving the EU, and fuels generally must be produced within the EU or in a country with a linked carbon market.
Cost Rankings on Intra-EU Routes
Combined, the three instruments push several alternative fuels below the cost of very low sulfur fuel oil on intra-EU voyages. At third-quarter 2026 prices, bioLNG costs more than double that of VLSFO before any incentives, yet it ends up at roughly half the cost of VLSFO once FuelEU credits and the proposed subsidy are factored in. Most of that advantage stems from FuelEU Maritime, and bioLNG would already undercut VLSFO without SMAP. Since bioLNG is a drop-in fuel for liquefied natural gas engines, this reinforces the business case for LNG dual-fuel ships trading in Europe. Renewable fuels of non-biological origin receive the most generous treatment of all and, on paper, EU-produced e-ammonia could become the cheapest fuel on intra-EU routes, although very few vessels can burn ammonia today and EU output remains limited.
Waste-Based Biofuels Left Out
The most obvious losers are liquid biofuels made from waste oils and fats. Used cooking oil and category 1 and 2 animal fats satisfy every EU sustainability test and earn full credit under both the ETS and FuelEU Maritime, but SMAP covers only advanced biofuels made from feedstocks listed in Annex IX Part A of the revised Renewable Energy Directive. Biogas, in contrast, appears eligible irrespective of feedstock.
The exclusion matters given the structure of Europe’s biodiesel industry. By 2030, crops and waste lipids such as used cooking oil and other waste fats and oils are projected to make up about 96% of the region’s biodiesel and renewable diesel production capacity, leaving only around 2% clearly eligible for support. Aviation’s sustainable fuel mandate draws on the same waste lipids, meaning shipping is unlikely to secure much eligible liquid biofuel.

articles.title: How Long Does It Take For A Laser Beam To Reach The Moon? - SlashGear
articles.summary: How Long Does It Take For A Laser Beam To Reach The Moon?  SlashGear
articles.full_text:
On average, the Moon is around 238,855 miles from Earth. Depending on where it is in its orbit, it can be as close as 226,000 miles or as far away as 251,000 miles. With a radius of approximately 1,080 miles, it's the fifth-largest moon in our solar system, but it's only one-third as wide as the big blue marble we call home. For a better visual reference, think of Earth as the diameter of a nickel and the Moon as that of a small pea or coffee bean. Roughly 30 nickels, or Earth-sized planets, would fit between the two.
We're not delving into how a laser works, but know that a laser's tightly packed beam is very different from the scattered light emitted by a bulb or flashlight. The very word "laser" isn't a word at all, but an acronym for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. A laser beam, which doesn't occur naturally, is made of individual particles of light energy called photons. This tightly focused stream of coherent light waves will travel in one direction without scattering. So, if the beam were fired into space, it would continue forever until it hit a solid object like the Moon.
Aside from the ever-expanding universe, nothing can go faster than the speed of light, at least as we currently understand it. That universal speed limit is 670,616,629.3844 miles per hour. Even though laser light differs from normal light, it's still light. Therefore, it would take a laser beam between 1.21 and 1.35 seconds to reach the Moon, again depending on where it is on its celestial trajectory.
Bouncing lasers off the Moon
Ah, but these numbers aren't just derived from a mathematical equation; they've been measured in real life. Unless you're a hardcore astrophile, you may not realize that five reflecting panels are currently sitting on the Moon. These panels have what scientists call "corner cube" mirrors attached to them because they're literally corners of a glass cube that can reflect light back to its source, no matter where it came from. See where we're going here?
The first was deposited by Apollo 11 astronauts in 1969, which had a total of 100 corner cubes. The Soviets dropped their first robotic rover (Lunokhod 1) in 1970, which had 14 mirrors. In 1971, the Apollo 14 crew placed one with 100 corner cubes, while the Apollo 15 crew placed another with 300. The Soviet Lunokhod 2 (with 14 mirrors) was left in 1973. The goal was to shoot a laser beam from Earth to the Moon to track the distance between them over time. On average, light takes about 2.5 seconds to make a round trip. As it turns out, these two celestial bodies are actually drifting about 1.5 inches apart every year.
But those old mirrors were starting to get dirty, likely caused by moon dust kicked up by tiny meteorite impacts. So, in June 2009, NASA launched the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) to study our nearest celestial body from its own orbit. Attached was a new, improved, clean reflector that NASA said was "the size of a paperback novel." Interestingly, it took over a decade to get a beam to hit its mark, but it finally did so in August 2020.

articles.title: Ireland urges greater efforts to save nature at global biodiversity summit - The Irish Times
articles.summary: Ireland urges greater efforts to save nature at global biodiversity summit  The Irish Times
articles.full_text:
Irish wildlife champions are among thousands of politicians, officials, academics, campaigners, conservationists, industrialists and finance chiefs attending the Global Biodiversity Summit – or Cop17 – in Yerevan, Armenia.
Their task at the global summit, which started on October 19th and runs until next Friday, is to examine how a commitment made four years ago to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030 is playing out. Following on from this, they will aim to put in place supports to ensure it can be realised.
That commitment came 30 years after the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro produced the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). Under the convention, the world undertook to protect nature and use its resources sustainably and fairly.
In the three decades that followed, those promises were broken repeatedly, universally and disastrously.
READ MORE
So what has happened since 2022 when a renewed effort was pledged?
A World Wildlife Fund report published just before Yerevan put the loss of wildlife populations at 73 per cent in 50 years and said the “vast decline in nature at a global scale” was continuing.
The secretariat of the CBD said similar in their pre-summit report.
“Many of the critical elements of progress, including finance, capacity, co-operation and data are still missing in action,” UN secretary-general Antonio Guterres remarked.
“Nature won’t thrive on good intentions,” he warned.
Ireland can’t hide from those remarks. An assessment last year showed 90 per cent of protected habitats – and the plants and animals dependent on them – were unhealthy.
But the Irish government – when the Green Party was part of it – led the charge in a tough battle for the European Parliament to pass the landmark Nature Restoration Law in 2024, establishing aims that mirror the global 2022 agreement.
Ireland then became the first member state to submit its mandatory national Nature Restoration Plan to the EU.
So can Ireland and the EU hold their heads high at the Yerevan negotiations?
Fintan Kelly of the Irish Environmental Network is there with representatives of Fair Seas, the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group, BirdWatch Ireland, the Irish Wildlife Trust and Streamscapes. He acknowledges the good intentions but holds the same fears as Guterres.
“The EU will arrive to the table and say, ‘look, we’ve got this world-leading law, we’re in the process of implementing it, member states have their national plans so trust us, we’re doing this’. But we’re there to point out this isn’t the full picture,” he said.
Kelly cites the ending of the EU’s LIFE projects, which have been critical for localised nature restoration. He also criticises the lack of funding for environmental protection in the new Common Agricultural Policy package and the proposed weakening of environmental assessment requirements in the Birds and Habitats Directives.
The next seven-year EU budget currently under negotiation also proposes cuts in funding for the environment and there is no EU-wide, or Irish, fund to support action under the Nature Restoration Law yet.
“We want to set up meetings with MEPs and point out we’re really concerned about the direction of travel,” Kelly said of the campaigning opportunities the Irish organisations hope to grab while in Yerevan.
Jane Stout, professor of ecology at Trinity College Dublin, has just returned from Yerevan and describes the first week of negotiations as “a mixed bag” of positivity and concern.
“The positivity is around the fact that all the governments are there and the reach of the CBD is expanding,” she said. “When it was first ratified back in 1992, for example, private businesses were not even mentioned and they were seen very much as the problem. Now they’re seen as part of the solution, so there were lots of sessions on business and biodiversity.
“On the one side, that’s positive and hopeful because it’s bringing more people into the conversation. On the other side, it’s a reflection of the fact that they’re starting to worry that this isn’t just an environmental problem.”
Stout is referring to the belated realisation that once water becomes too polluted to use and soils too depleted to grow anything, once pollinators disappear and oceans stop supporting marine life, almost every industry loses its raw materials and the vital services that nature provides.
Wrangling finance out of industry and the richer countries to support a turnaround in nature’s fortunes is a key focus of the summit.
Minister for Nature Christopher O’Sullivan is in Yerevan and acknowledges Ireland has yet to put its own money where its good intentions lie.
“I have been working with colleagues across Government to establish a dedicated nature restoration fund for a number of months,” he said, adding he hoped to “be in a position to share more information soon”.
On the wider issues, he said his approach to the talks would be to emphasise what is at stake.
“We’re not on track to meet our 2030 targets, [which is] putting people, the economy and the wider environment – as well as wildlife and habitats – at risk of significant consequences,” he said.
“What we’re saying, as both the EU and as Ireland, is that we can’t give up. We need to do more. We need to work together to change this awful trajectory and protect the diversity of life on this amazing planet.”

articles.title: Green Hiring Grows 25% as Green Talent Rises Only 13%, LinkedIn Report Finds
articles.summary:
Demand for green skills is growing twice as fast as supply, according to LinkedIn’s Global Green Skills Report 2026. The professional networking platform found the share of green hiring rose […]
The post Green Hiring Grows 25% as Green Talent Rises Only 13%, LinkedIn Report Finds appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Green Hiring Grows 25% as Green Talent Rises Only 13%, LinkedIn Report Finds
- Demand outpaces supply: The share of green hiring rose 25% year-on-year, while green talent grew 13%.
- Beyond green titles: Nearly three in four green hires (74%) go into roles without traditionally green titles.
- Gender gap persists: Women make up three in ten workers with green skills.
Demand for green skills is growing twice as fast as supply, according to LinkedIn’s Global Green Skills Report 2026. The professional networking platform found the share of green hiring rose 25% year-on-year. Meanwhile, the share of green talent in the workforce grew 13%. LinkedIn published the report ahead of COP31 and called the skills gap a worsening bottleneck.
Green-skilled workers are hired at more than 1.5 times the rate of the wider workforce. Most green hires go to roles without traditionally green titles. Financial Services added green skills fastest, at 18% a year, followed by Technology and Media (15%) and Retail (14%)
The share of data centre workers with at least one green skill rose from 4% in 2021 to 14% in 2026, the report says. Over the same period, green workers with AI skills grew 54% a year. But Adam Elman, Head of Sustainability for EMEA at Google, noted in a LinkedIn post that the median share is still only 4.2%. “We need to limit AI’s environmental impact, but AI also brings a huge opportunity to advance sustainability,” Elman wrote.
Demand outpaces supply in every industry LinkedIn measures, and the company warns shortages could hold back climate targets. As a result, it is calling on governments, employers and education providers to act. “Green skills are no longer a niche. They’re how businesses build efficiency, manage risk, and stay competitive. Demand for them is now outpacing supply in every industry we measure, and that makes talent the bottleneck for progress. Ambition alone won’t upgrade a grid, retrofit a home, or make a data center more efficient – people will. Governments and employers must treat green skills as core economic infrastructure and invest in training now, or workers will miss out on the jobs, growth and economic opportunity the transition presents,” said Sue Duke, Managing Director for EMEA and Global Vice President of Public Policy at LinkedIn.
Age and Gender Gaps
Gen Z’s share of workers with green skills has grown 17% a year since 2021, against 9% for Millennials. Also, 57% of surveyed Gen Z workers want a climate or energy transition job. Yet 54% find it difficult to land a green job, compared with 26% of Millennials.
At the current rate, LinkedIn estimates the gender gap in green skills will take more than 30 years to close. LinkedIn did not disclose the report’s methodology, sample size or data period.
RELATED ARTICLE: Job Seekers with Green Skills 54.6% More Likely to Get Hired in 2024: LinkedIn Report
Who It Affects
- Governments: Asked to include workforce readiness in the second Global Stocktake, a UN climate review ending at COP33 in 2028.
- Employers: Urged to hire on skills, not qualifications or job titles, which LinkedIn says could grow the green talent pool 3.5 times.
- Education providers: Asked to build green and AI skills into existing courses, apprenticeships and workplace training.

articles.title: EIB Group Sets €30 Billion Adaptation Finance Goal for 2026-2030, Doubling Its Previous Five Years
articles.summary:
The European Investment Bank (EIB) Group will provide at least €30 billion in climate adaptation finance from 2026 to 2030. That doubles the roughly €15 billion it delivered under its […]
The post EIB Group Sets €30 Billion Adaptation Finance Goal for 2026-2030, Doubling Its Previous Five Years appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
EIB Group Sets €30 Billion Adaptation Finance Goal for 2026-2030, Doubling Its Previous Five Years
- €30 billion goal: At least €30 billion in adaptation finance for 2026-2030, double the 2021-2025 total.
- Smaller borrowers: Support targets SMEs, farmers, cities, vulnerable communities and climate-vulnerable partner countries.
- Free data tool: ClimateSET will give clients free, location-specific climate risk data.
The European Investment Bank (EIB) Group will provide at least €30 billion in climate adaptation finance from 2026 to 2030. That doubles the roughly €15 billion it delivered under its first adaptation plan, which covered 2021 to 2025. Its new Climate Adaptation Plan Phase 2 shifts the focus from raising awareness to scaling up investment. The plan supports the European Commission’s resilience agenda and forms part of the EIB’s Climate Bank Roadmap Phase 2.
According to the EIB, adaptation investment is not keeping pace with growing climate risks. It estimates the EU needs about €70 billion a year to 2050, against roughly €29 billion invested today. The plan also warns that savings are not flowing sufficiently into resilience projects, and investable pipelines remain insufficient. Yet research cited in the plan finds that each euro spent on adaptation can generate up to €10 in benefits.
The plan rests on three pillars: scaling up investment, investing where resilience matters most and mainstreaming resilience across operations. To build pipelines, the Group will pair loans with advisory work, blended finance (public grants mixed with private capital) and risk-sharing tools. Priority sectors include water, energy, transport and communication networks, flood protection and early warning systems. Beyond the EU, its external arm EIB Global will focus on Small Island Developing States and Least Developed Countries.
What’s New Since Phase One
Under the first plan, annual EIB adaptation volumes almost quadrupled, and climate risk management became a core part of operations. Phase 2 adds ClimateSET, a free web tool built with the Copernicus Climate Change Service that maps location-specific climate hazards. The Group will also widen its Green Checker tool to more adaptation activities, easing access to intermediated finance for small businesses. However, the plan sets no annual interim milestones and does not say how the €30 billion will split between EU and partner countries.
RELATED ARTICLE: EIB Invests $46 Million in Modular Nuclear
Why It Matters
For the EIB Group, the plan backs the €30 billion goal with a delivery channel for smaller borrowers. That channel is the Green Gateway, which bundles intermediated lending, risk-sharing and advisory support for SMEs and farmers. This positions the Group to grow adaptation volumes through national promotional banks and commercial lenders, provided they can bring forward enough bankable projects.

articles.title: Masdar Buys 550+ MW Greek Solar Project From Lightsource bp, Plans Battery Storage
articles.summary:
Masdar has agreed to acquire and develop a 550+ megawatt (MW) solar photovoltaic (PV) project in Greece from Lightsource bp. Masdar calls it one of Greece’s largest solar projects. The […]
The post Masdar Buys 550+ MW Greek Solar Project From Lightsource bp, Plans Battery Storage appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Masdar Buys 550+ MW Greek Solar Project From Lightsource bp, Plans Battery Storage
- Solar acquisition: Masdar will buy a 550+ MW Greek solar project from Lightsource bp.
- Battery storage: Masdar plans to add storage to support grid stability.
- Data center MoU: Masdar and Khazna will explore green data centers in Greece.
Masdar has agreed to acquire and develop a 550+ megawatt (MW) solar photovoltaic (PV) project in Greece from Lightsource bp. Masdar calls it one of Greece’s largest solar projects. The plant is set to start operating by the end of 2026. It will produce enough electricity to power more than 200,000 homes a year.
The deal was announced during a visit to Greece by His Highness Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi. The UAE and Greece are marking more than 50 years of diplomatic relations. Masdar says the project will help meet Greek electricity demand growth driven by artificial intelligence (AI) and digital infrastructure.
Separately, Masdar and Khazna Data Centers signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on green data center development in Greece. The pact pairs Khazna’s data center development and operating skills with Masdar’s renewable energy and storage expertise. The partners will explore dedicated clean power and storage for Greece’s growing digital infrastructure needs. “The UAE and Greece share a strategic partnership built on trust, long-term ambition and a commitment to mutual prosperity. As artificial intelligence and digital industries transform the global economy, access to reliable, affordable energy will be increasingly critical to competitiveness and growth. Masdar’s expanding renewable energy portfolio, alongside its new collaboration with Khazna, brings together two essential foundations of the future economy: clean power and digital infrastructure. Together, these initiatives will strengthen Greece’s energy security, support its ambition to become a regional digital hub and unlock new opportunities for investment and economic growth. They also reflect the UAE’s commitment to building enduring international partnerships that power the industries of tomorrow and deliver lasting prosperity,” said His Excellency Dr Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber, UAE Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and Chairman of Masdar.
Battery Storage and Substations
Masdar plans to add battery storage to support grid stability and power system flexibility. The deal also includes two privately owned substations linking the project to the electricity transmission system. It still needs regulatory approval and customary closing conditions, with completion expected by the end of this year. Masdar did not disclose the purchase price, offtakers or any impact on employees.
RELATED ARTICLE: Masdar, Taaleri Open 154MW Serbia Wind Farm
Building on TERNA ENERGY
The acquisition is Masdar’s first strategic investment through TERNA ENERGY, its platform for Southeastern and Central Europe. Masdar took full ownership in April 2025, after a 70 per cent purchase valued the company at €3.2 billion. Masdar targets 6 gigawatts (GW) of regional operational capacity by 2030, backed by a €5.5 billion plan. “These agreements represent another important milestone in our European growth strategy, expanding our portfolio with a high-quality solar asset that we will develop further with battery storage, and will deliver stable, long-term returns. Our collaboration with Khazna builds on this foundation, exploring opportunities to power Greece’s growing digital economy with clean energy. Through TERNA ENERGY, we are building a stronger renewable energy platform in Greece and the wider region, while creating long-term value for our shareholders, partners and the communities we serve,” said Mohamed Jameel Al Ramahi, Chief Executive Officer of Masdar.
Why It Matters
For Masdar, the deal adds a large solar and storage asset to TERNA ENERGY’s portfolio in Greece. For Khazna, the MoU adds Masdar’s renewable and storage expertise to its Greek data center plans. If the MoU yields supply agreements, the project could become a contracted clean power source for Khazna’s Greek data centers.

articles.title: BlackRock’s Akaysha Energy Refinances Four Australian Batteries With $1.23 Billion Portfolio Facility
articles.summary:
Akaysha Energy has secured an $1.23 billion debt facility from a consortium of 11 banks. The facility refinances existing project-level debt on four Australian battery assets into one portfolio-level structure. […]
The post BlackRock’s Akaysha Energy Refinances Four Australian Batteries With $1.23 Billion Portfolio Facility appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
BlackRock’s Akaysha Energy Refinances Four Australian Batteries With $1.23 Billion Portfolio Facility
- Portfolio refinancing: Akaysha Energy has secured an $1.23 billion debt facility from 11 banks.
- Four assets combined: Debt on Brendale, Ulinda Park, Orana and Elaine moves into one portfolio-level structure.
- Pipeline flexibility: Akaysha says the facility supports a roughly 6 GW / 25 GWh Australian development pipeline.
Akaysha Energy has secured an $1.23 billion debt facility from a consortium of 11 banks. The facility refinances existing project-level debt on four Australian battery assets into one portfolio-level structure. As a result, the developer can finance a growing asset base rather than arranging debt project by project. Founded in 2021, Melbourne-based Akaysha was acquired in 2022 by BlackRock’s Climate Infrastructure business, part of BlackRock Real Assets.
The four assets are the Brendale and Ulinda Park batteries in Queensland and the Orana battery in New South Wales. The fourth is the Elaine project in Victoria, which began construction in October 2025. Elaine is expected to be completed in the second half of 2027, while the other three already operate. The financing consists of three facilities with five-, seven- and ten-year terms, plus revolving liquidity and contingent instrument facilities.
The lenders are ANZ, BNP Paribas, Bank of China, CIBC, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Deutsche Bank, DNB, ING, Mizuho, MUFG and Rabobank. Akaysha did not disclose the facility’s pricing or how it is split among the lenders. “We are delighted to support this transaction, drawing on our project finance expertise to bring operational and construction-stage assets into one structure that meets the needs of a growing battery storage portfolio,” said Rachel Chia, Head of Project Finance, APAC at Deutsche Bank.
Akaysha says the deal gives it flexibility to advance about 6 GW / 25 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS). These projects sit across the National Electricity Market (NEM), the grid serving eastern Australia. In Victoria, the pipeline includes the Glenrowan and Deer Park projects. It also includes Murray Terminal and Kilnacroft Creek in New South Wales, and Oaky Creek in Queensland. “As well as refinancing our existing operating and construction assets, this portfolio-level facility gives us the flexibility to accelerate our next wave of projects while we continue deploying capital where we see the strongest opportunities across the pipeline,” said Andrew Wegman, Managing Director and Chief Financial & Investment Officer of Akaysha Energy.
What’s New Since Waratah
The facility closes weeks after Akaysha’s Waratah Super Battery reached completion and began operating at full capacity. Sized at 850 MW and 1,680 MWh, Waratah is described as the most powerful machine of any type on the Australian grid.
RELATED ARTICLE: Akaysha Energy Secures $196M Debt Facility to Expand Battery Storage Portfolio
Why It Matters
The facility gives Akaysha one debt structure covering three operating batteries and one under construction, with terms of up to ten years. That positions Akaysha to move pipeline projects such as Glenrowan, Deer Park and Oaky Creek into construction sooner. That outcome depends on the 11 lenders agreeing to bring new assets into the portfolio structure.

articles.title: GHG Protocol Board Backs Two Scope 2 Methods, Phasing Companies Toward Hourly-Matched Claims
articles.summary:
GHG Protocol’s Independent Standards Board (ISB) has proposed two market-based methods for companies reporting scope 2 emissions. Method 1 would require hourly matching, deliverability and incrementality, while Method 2 keeps […]
The post GHG Protocol Board Backs Two Scope 2 Methods, Phasing Companies Toward Hourly-Matched Claims appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
GHG Protocol Board Backs Two Scope 2 Methods, Phasing Companies Toward Hourly-Matched Claims
- Two-method framework: The ISB proposed a new hourly-matched method alongside the existing 2015 market-based rules.
- Method 1 cut-off: After a date still to be set, market-based reporters shall use Method 1 where qualifying data exists.
- Next milestones: A consolidated consultation is slated for Q2 2027, with a joint GHG Protocol-ISO standard due in Q4 2028.
GHG Protocol’s Independent Standards Board (ISB) has proposed two market-based methods for companies reporting scope 2 emissions. Method 1 would require hourly matching, deliverability and incrementality, while Method 2 keeps the 2015 Scope 2 Guidance rules. However, companies may use Method 2 only until a date still to be set. The proposals are due for consolidated public consultation in Q2 2027.
Under the ISB’s September 2026 direction, companies would report market-based emissions if data meeting quality criteria is available. Whether that reporting is required, recommended or optional is still open. Before the cut-off, companies should use Method 1 and shall disclose which method they apply.
Method 1 counts energy attribute certificates (EACs), which certify clean power output, only if they match hourly consumption. The certificates must also come from a grid region where the company uses power. Incrementality further limits claims to plants built within a set number of years. The update did not set the transition date, the incrementality window or the data quality criteria.
What Changed Since the Consultation
The consultation draft, open from October 20, 2025 to January 31, 2026, applied hourly matching and deliverability to all market-based claims. GHG Protocol said the 2015 method lets companies claim reductions from projects on grids disconnected from their operations. But feedback split between backers of hourly, local procurement and backers of annual matching across broad geographies. As a result, ISB members backed two methods with differentiated requirements and claims in July 2026.
Next Steps
The Scope 2 Technical Working Group (TWG) will develop proposed revisions at an in-person workshop. Deliverability, incrementality, feasibility and implementation timing are the key issues. The ISB must then approve the revisions before they enter consultation.
RELATED ARTICLE: GHG Protocol and IFRS Foundation Partner to Enhance GHG Emissions Reporting Standards
Who It Affects
- Market-based scope 2 reporters: After the cut-off, they shall use Method 1 if data meeting the quality criteria is available.
- Buyers of annually matched or distant EACs: Purchases outside future rules may move to a GHG Impact Statement or non-GHG indicators under the Actions and Market Instruments (AMI) framework.
- Scope 1 and 3 reporters: The Q2 2027 consultation will also cover proposed scope 1, scope 3 and AMI requirements.

articles.title: Morgan Stanley Survey Finds Only 2% of Asset Owners Expect Large Sustainable Allocation Gains
articles.summary:
Morgan Stanley’s 2026 Sustainable Signals survey finds institutional investors still plan to grow sustainable allocations, but more slowly. More than eight in 10 asset owners and asset managers expect to […]
The post Morgan Stanley Survey Finds Only 2% of Asset Owners Expect Large Sustainable Allocation Gains appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Morgan Stanley Survey Finds Only 2% of Asset Owners Expect Large Sustainable Allocation Gains
- Allocations still rising: More than eight in 10 institutional investors plan to raise sustainable allocations, but few expect big increases.
- Data concerns climb: 64% call data availability and consistency a very significant concern, up from 47%.
- Adaptation leads themes: Climate adaptation and resilience has overtaken mitigation as investors’ top sustainability theme.
Morgan Stanley’s 2026 Sustainable Signals survey finds institutional investors still plan to grow sustainable allocations, but more slowly. More than eight in 10 asset owners and asset managers expect to raise allocations over the next two years. However, only 2% of asset owners and 4% of asset managers expect growth above 10 percentage points. In 2025, around one-fifth expected gains that large.
The Morgan Stanley Institute for Sustainable Investing polled 900 institutional investors between August and October 2026. Respondents are in North America, Europe and Asia Pacific, and all practice or plan to practice sustainable investing. Morgan Stanley did not disclose how responses split by region or investor type. “Our annual global survey of institutional investors indicates that a majority expect to increase sustainable investment allocations in the coming years, recognizing growth opportunities and the rising materiality of sustainability-related risks,” said Jessica Alsford, Chief Sustainability Officer and Chair of the Institute for Sustainable Investing at Morgan Stanley.
Quick anonymous worklife pollWhat's my daily work emissions burn, or savings?Powered by ESG News
Concerns Ease, but Data Worries Grow
On average, 27% of investors rated the survey’s concerns as very significant, down from 38% in 2025. Concern about negative media or public views of sustainable investing fell from 34% to 8%. Data is the exception, with 64% calling data availability and consistency a very significant concern, up from 47%.
Meanwhile, more than two-thirds cite portfolio risk reduction as a reason to invest sustainably, up from half in 2025. More than 90% also consider sustainability important to managing investment risk. “In 2026, a consistent picture has emerged across our Sustainable Signals series – with individuals, corporates and institutional investors all showing high levels of continued commitment to sustainability, yet at a more measured pace and with a sharper focus on managing risk,” Alsford said.
Adaptation and AI Move Up the Agenda
Climate adaptation and resilience is now the most common theme, cited by 59%, ahead of climate mitigation at 52%. However, almost 90% find the impact of physical climate change on their assets hard to evaluate, up from 66%. Most still expect physical climate risks to affect asset prices within five years.
Two-thirds of respondents include responsible AI in their sustainable investing strategy. Most focus on how companies govern their AI use, rather than on large language model (LLM) providers.
RELATED ARTICLE: Morgan Stanley Selects 24 Ventures for 2026 Cohort
Who It Affects
- Asset managers: Asset owners hold 41% of externally managed sustainable assets in customized mandates or separately managed accounts. Also, 86% expect that share to rise, citing more control over strategy and timing.
- Managers bidding for mandates: More than 90% of respondents say sustainable investing options are a key differentiator in awarding or winning mandates.
- Listed companies: Almost 90% of investors engage with companies, and 59% favor fewer, more substantive interactions. Over 60% rate private talks with management as very effective.

articles.title: Datamaran’s Applicability Assessment Rates Each Entity Against Active and Proposed Regulations
articles.summary:
Datamaran has made Applicability Assessment generally available as a new feature of its Regulatory Monitoring platform. With one click, the AI-assisted tool assesses every entity in a group against active […]
The post Datamaran’s Applicability Assessment Rates Each Entity Against Active and Proposed Regulations appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Datamaran’s Applicability Assessment Rates Each Entity Against Active and Proposed Regulations
- General availability: Datamaran launched Applicability Assessment within its Regulatory Monitoring platform.
- Three-way ratings: Each entity and regulation pairing is rated Likely, Unlikely, or Uncertain to apply.
- Expert review planned: A coming feature will let experts validate results and record their rationale.
Datamaran has made Applicability Assessment generally available as a new feature of its Regulatory Monitoring platform. With one click, the AI-assisted tool assesses every entity in a group against active and proposed mandatory regulations. Each pairing is then rated Likely, Unlikely, or Uncertain to apply.
Datamaran said that for organizations operating across multiple countries, identifying which regulations apply is still largely manual. Teams check hundreds of rules against thresholds one entity at a time, then repeat the work whenever something changes. The company warned that this process does not scale and that cutting corners risks missing obligations that matter. “‘We just need to know what applies to us’ is something we hear often from legal, compliance, and sustainability teams. Applicability Assessment provides that information quickly and reliably at the entity level at scale,” said Marjella Lecourt-Alma, CEO and co-founder of Datamaran.
Quick anonymous worklife pollWhat's my daily work emissions burn, or savings?Powered by ESG News
The feature pre-fills entity profiles with headquarters, countries of operation, sector, revenue, headcount, and more. Users can then group entities by region, business unit, supplier tier, or any other lens. A whole group can be assessed at once, starting from saved views, curated searches, or regulation notifications.
Results show the criteria behind each determination and flag the data needed to resolve Uncertain ratings. Meanwhile, a dashboard shows exposure by regulation and entity, and an audit trail tracks every change. Expert Review, listed as coming soon, will assign subject-matter experts to validate results.
Companies that piloted the tool before launch highlighted its transparent logic and ease of use. However, Datamaran did not name the pilot companies, disclose pricing, or give a release date for Expert Review. “Datamaran’s Applicability Assessment made the same determinations we would make, and I liked the logic. Being able to look at the assessment criteria and have that logic really laid out gives me confidence. And because we have a lot of different discrete organizations, being able to start from a dashboard is very valuable,” said a pilot user at a global industrial manufacturer. “The Applicability Assessment is really user-friendly and very straightforward to use. It calls out pretty clearly which data fields are missing, so we know exactly what’s needed to get to an answer,” said a pilot user at a global food manufacturer.
RELATED ARTICLE: Datamaran Launches Suite to Power Always-On ESG Strategy
From Discovery to Decision
Datamaran tracks mandatory regulations and voluntary initiatives across 99 non-financial topics and more than 190 countries. Because the assessments also cover proposed rules, companies can plan for obligations before they take effect. In one client study, research that took around 28 hours manually took five minutes with Datamaran.
Why It Matters
The launch moves Datamaran’s Regulatory Monitoring platform from tracking rules to determining which ones apply to each entity. It answers a request the company says it hears from legal, compliance, and sustainability teams. If pilot results hold across larger groups, the feature positions Datamaran to upsell existing clients that manage many discrete entities.
